Statistical inference

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Probability and statistics
OurBigBook.com Words: 29k Articles: 482
Statistical inference uses observed data and a statistical model to learn about unknown features of the process that generated them. In a parametric statistical model, write X∼Pθ​: the probability distribution depends on an unknown statistical parameter θ. An estimand specifies the target, such as a mean or a difference of means. A statistic is a function of the observations; an estimator is a statistic used to estimate the target. Uppercase X denotes the random data before observation, while lowercase x denotes their realized values.
Three questions lead to different outputs. Statistical estimation asks which target value the observations suggest. A confidence interval asks for a range produced by a procedure with calibrated coverage probability. A hypothesis test asks whether the observations depart sufficiently from a specified null hypothesis to enter its rejection region. These outputs complement one another: an estimated effect size describes magnitude, while a standard error describes the sampling distribution of an estimator. A p-value describes a tail probability under the null hypothesis.
The appeal of statistical inference is that it turns variable observations into reproducible uncertainty statements. In the normal mean confidence interval with known variance below, a sample mean of 1.2 has standard error 0.5: both the estimated shift and its precision matter. The calibration depends on the statistical model, including independence and the specified probability distribution. Increasing sample size improves precision under those assumptions; it does not repair a systematically misleading sampling procedure. Bayesian inference provides another framework, using a prior distribution and a likelihood function to obtain a posterior distribution.

Effect size

Words: 46
Statistical inference OurBigBook.com
An effect size measures the magnitude of an observed or modeled relationship. A standardized mean difference expresses a mean contrast in standard-deviation units; other effect sizes include a correlation coefficient or odds ratio. Magnitude is distinct from the evidence against a null hypothesis supplied by a p-value: a small effect size can have a small p-value in a sufficiently large sample.

Statistical process control

Words: 445 Articles: 7
Statistical inference OurBigBook.com
Statistical process control compares observed process outcomes with a stable reference model and control limits reflecting expected sampling variation. An observation outside those limits is a signal to investigate, not proof of a specific cause. Varying sample volumes require varying limits, and multiple testing changes the chance of a chance signal somewhere in the display.

CUSUM (Ct​=max(0,Ct−1​+Wt​))

Words: 223 Articles: 3
Statistical process control OurBigBook.com
A CUSUM accumulates evidence for a change in a monitored probability distribution. With Wt​ a log-likelihood ratio increment favoring a specified changed distribution, reset the accumulated score at zero and signal when it exceeds a chosen boundary h. For C0​=0, Ct​ is the largest nonnegative sum of successive increments ending at t. This permits repeated detection of a change with an unknown onset, rather than a single fixed-start test.

Poisson likelihood-ratio CUSUM (Wt​=Yt​logθ−(θ−1)λ0t​)

Words: 48
CUSUM OurBigBook.com
For independent Poisson observations, comparing mean λ0t​ with θλ0t​ gives the displayed log-likelihood ratio. Updating a CUSUM with these scores targets the specified multiplicative increase. Its expected score is negative under the null and positive under the alternative when θ>1, so resetting at zero discards earlier evidence against an increase.

Average run length (ARL=Einf{t≥1:Ct​≥h})

Words: 52
CUSUM OurBigBook.com
The average run length of a CUSUM is the expectation of its first signalling time under a specified data model and initial chart state. A large in-control average run length discourages false alarms; a small out-of-control value indicates rapid detection. The mean alone does not give a finite-horizon Type I error probability or the complete detection-delay distribution.

Fast initial response CUSUM (0<C0​<h)

Jackknife resampling

Words: 645 Articles: 2
Statistical inference OurBigBook.com
The delete-one form of jackknife resampling recalculates a statistic after deleting each observation in turn. It uses one observed statistical sample to investigate how sensitive an estimator is to its individual observations, and supplies both a jackknife variance estimator and jackknife bias correction. The calculations are deterministic once the data are fixed: no random draws are needed.
In the basic setting, X1​,…,Xn​ are independent and identically distributed random variables, with sample size n>1. Let x1​,…,xn​ be the observed values and θn​=tn​(x1​,…,xn​) a scalar estimator of an estimand θ. Apply the same estimation rule to each reduced statistical sample, using its new sample size n−1 wherever the rule requires it:
θ(−i)​=tn−1​(x1​,…,xi−1​,xi+1​,…,xn​),i=1,…,n,θJ​=n1​∑i=1n​θ(−i)​.
(1)
Every index is deleted exactly once; an unusual value is treated by the same rule as every other value. The mean θJ​ summarizes the deletion estimates. They overlap in n−2 observations, so they are generally not independent random variables representing fresh repetitions of the original experiment. Cosma Shalizi's [ref] explain this construction and its scaling.
For a concrete sample mean, use the data (1,2,3,4,10), whose full sample mean is x=4. The five deletion sample means, in observation order, are
(θ(−1)​,…,θ(−5)​)=(4.75,4.5,4.25,4,2.5),θJ​=4.
(2)
Deleting 1 raises the sample mean by 0.75, while deleting 10 lowers the sample mean by 1.5. Thus 10 has the largest deletion effect in this statistical sample. This is a descriptive sensitivity calculation, not a rule for removing that observation: the full sample mean remains 4.
Early literature includes M. H. Quenouille's [ref] and John W. Tukey's one-paragraph abstract [ref], within the issue's collected abstracts. Shalizi's [ref] discuss the later development of jackknife bias correction and the jackknife variance estimator.

Jackknife variance estimator (VJ​)

Words: 325 Articles: 1
Jackknife resampling OurBigBook.com
The jackknife variance estimator estimates the sampling variance of the full-data estimator, using the deletion estimates and their mean from jackknife resampling:
VJ​=nn−1​∑i=1n​(θ(−i)​−θJ​)2,SEJ​=VJ​​.
(3)
The square root is the estimated standard error. The factor n−1 multiplies the divisor-n variance of the deletion estimates: those estimates vary less than estimates from new independent experiments because almost all their observations are shared. Ryan Tibshirani's [ref] give the same scaling in terms of the divisor-(n−1) sample variance of the deletion estimates.
For the sample mean, this formula has an exact algebraic simplification. With sn2​ denoting the usual sample variance,
θ(−i)​=n−1nx−xi​​,θJ​=x,θ(−i)​−θJ​=−n−1xi​−x​,
(4)
and therefore
VJ​=n(n−1)1​∑i=1n​(xi​−x)2=nsn2​​.
(5)
Under the independent and identically distributed assumption and a finite second moment, sn2​ is an unbiased estimator of the population variance σ2. Consequently VJ​ is an unbiased estimator of the sample mean's sampling variance σ2/n. The equality VJ​=sn2​/n itself holds for any observed data with n>1; its sampling interpretation uses the stated assumptions.
For (1,2,3,4,10), the sum of squared deviations from the sample mean is 50, giving sample variance s52​=50/4=12.5. The deletion sample means have squared deviations totaling 3.125, so
VJ​=54​(3.125)=2.5=512.5​,SEJ​=2.5​≈1.58114.
(6)
Here 12.5 estimates the variance of individual observations, while 2.5 estimates the sampling variance of their sample mean. These answer different questions.
For more general statistics, validity requires regularity beyond the deletion formula, such as a sufficiently smooth function of sample means with suitable moments. Ordinary delete-one jackknife resampling can fail for nonsmooth quantiles, including the median; see Larry Wasserman's [ref]. With statistical dependence, deleting individual observations need not reproduce the relevant sampling variance; the deletion scheme must reflect that statistical dependence. Shalizi's [ref] distinguish the basic independent and identically distributed case from extensions.

Fisherian conditional inference

Statistical inference OurBigBook.com
In a parametric statistical model, the likelihood function compares parameter values, while sampling distributions calibrate tests and confidence intervals. A sufficient statistic retains the parameter information. Conditioning on an observed ancillary statistic restricts that calibration to experiments with the same ancillary configuration, instead of averaging over configurations whose distribution is unrelated to the parameter. Since the ancillary's marginal law is parameter-free, conditional and unconditional likelihoods have the same parameter-dependent factor. With a nuisance parameter, a conditional law or pivotal quantity must remove it before inference for the parameter of interest can use a nuisance-free reference law.

Fisherian conditional inference OurBigBook.com
When an experiment's configuration is observed, inference conditions on the experiment actually performed rather than averaging over its possible configurations. Conditioning on an ancillary statistic is a central application; freedom from a nuisance parameter must still be checked in the resulting conditional distribution.

Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

Words: 1k Articles: 3
Statistical inference OurBigBook.com
The one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test checks goodness of fit by comparing an empirical distribution function Fn​ with a specified cumulative distribution function F0​. Its Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic Dn​ is the largest vertical gap anywhere between the two curves. Every threshold asks the same concrete question: what proportion of the observations are at or below it, and what probability does the proposed probability distribution assign there? A large discrepancy supplies evidence against the null hypothesis.
For example, four stipulated observations (1/10,2/5,4/5,9/10) compared with the uniform distribution on [0,1] give D4​=3/10. Just before 4/5, only two observations have been counted, so the empirical distribution function approaches 1/2, while F0​ approaches 4/5. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic section calculates every jump-side gap. These are exact illustrative numbers, not experimental measurements or a claim of statistical significance.
The ordinary one-sample calibration assumes independent and identically distributed real observations and a simple hypothesis H0​:F=F0​, with F0​ a continuous function fixed before inspecting these observations. All statistical parameters of F0​ must be specified.[ref] Under that null hypothesis, the probability integral transform gives Ui​=F0​(Xi​) with the uniform distribution on (0,1), retaining independence. Consequently the sampling distribution of Dn​ depends on the sample size n, but not on the particular continuous F0​. This is the useful sense in which the calibration is distribution-free.
For the exponential distribution of rate one, F0​(x)=1−e−x for x≥0. Take xi​=−log(1−ui​) for the four stipulated ui​ above. The probability integral transform changes the horizontal coordinates but preserves both the order statistics and their cumulative heights, so the same Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic 3/10 appears on both scales. More generally, for continuous F0​, the jump-side formulas depend only on F0​(X(i)​). Strict increase everywhere is unnecessary: intervals on which F0​ is constant have probability zero under the null hypothesis. This explains the invariance without assuming a strictly positive probability density function.
The observed Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is a discrepancy, whereas its p-value is a tail probability under the null hypothesis:
p=PrH0​​(Dnnew​≥dobs​).
(7)
Here Dnnew​ is computed from a fresh sample of the same sample size. Choose a significance level α before the test and reject when the calibrated p-value is at most α. The value D4​=3/10 alone supplies neither a p-value nor a rejection decision. Failure to reject does not establish that the null hypothesis is true. A finite-sample calibration and the asymptotic Kolmogorov-Smirnov theorem are distinct; a cutoff for Dn​ must be rescaled before use with n​Dn​.[ref]
Fitting statistical parameters on the tested observations replaces F0​ by the random Fθ​. The resulting transformed observations need not be independent and identically distributed uniforms, so the ordinary reference law fails. The Lilliefors test addresses a particular fitted normal distribution. More general parametric bootstrap calibration must simulate from the fitted statistical model and repeat the fitting in every replicate; holding the fitted statistical parameters fixed during those comparisons calibrates a different procedure. Such a parametric bootstrap requires its own validity justification rather than inheriting exactness from the simple-null test.
For a discrete probability distribution, F0​(X) is generally not uniform. Equal observations also arise from rounding, so tied data require a calibration that accounts for the discrete probability distribution or the rounding rule. The discrepancy remains meaningful, but continuous-null p-values are not automatically valid. Statistical dependence likewise changes the reference law. The two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test compares two empirical distribution functions and has a different calibration.[ref]

For an empirical distribution function Fn​ and a specified cumulative distribution function F0​, the one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is their Kolmogorov distance:
Fn​(x)=n1​∑j=1n​1{Xj​≤x}​,Dn​=supx∈R​∣Fn​(x)−F0​(x)∣.
(8)
The displayed sum uses an indicator function. With this convention, Fn​ is right-continuous. For distinct observations, its value and its left one-sided limit at the ith order statistic are Fn​(X(i)​)=i/n and Fn​(X(i)−​)=(i−1)/n.
For continuous F0​, both jump sides matter. Define the two directional discrepancies by
Dn+​=supx​(Fn​(x)−F0​(x))=max1≤i≤n​{ni​−F0​(X(i)​)},
(9)
Dn−​=supx​(F0​(x)−Fn​(x))=max1≤i≤n​{F0​(X(i)​)−ni−1​},Dn​=max(Dn+​,Dn−​).
(10)
Thus Dn+​ uses the empirical distribution function immediately after a jump, and Dn−​ uses its left one-sided limit.[ref] A supremum need not be attained.
For n=4, F0​(x)=x on [0,1], and the stipulated order statistics (1/10,2/5,4/5,9/10), the complete calculation is
i1234​X(i)​1/102/54/59/10​F4​(X(i)−​)01/41/23/4​F4​(X(i)​)1/41/23/41​i/4−F0​(X(i)​)3/201/10−1/201/10​F0​(X(i)​)−(i−1)/41/103/203/103/20​​
(11)
The last two columns give the signed directional gaps: D4+​=3/20, D4−​=3/10, and D4​=3/10. In contrast, checking only ∣F4​(X(i)​)−F0​(X(i)​)∣ gives 3/20 and misses the largest gap approached as x↑4/5. At x=4/5 itself, the gap has already fallen to 1/20.
The finite formula follows from the behavior between jumps: the empirical distribution function Fn​ is constant and the cumulative distribution function F0​ is monotone, so the largest directional gaps occur at the two interval ends, possibly as one-sided limits. The two tails introduce no larger gap. Checking every jump side therefore gives the exact supremum.
A common normalized Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is n​Dn​, which equals 3/5 in this example. Its large-sample reference law comes from the Kolmogorov-Smirnov theorem. The unscaled Dn​ remains the largest difference of cumulative probabilities, not a p-value.
There is a useful exact exception to the usual warning about fitting statistical parameters. Suppose n≥2 independent and identically distributed observations have the uniform distribution on (0,θ) with unknown θ>0. Let M=maxi​Xi​ and let J be the label of its almost surely unique maximizing observation. Conditional on M=m and J=j, the surviving labelled observations (Xi​)i=j​ are independent with the uniform distribution on (0,m); after division by m they are independent and identically distributed uniforms on (0,1). These are conditional distributions defined by probability density functions, since the event M=m has probability zero.
To check this, the joint probability density function of M and J=j is mn−1/θn for 0<m<θ. Dividing the original joint probability density function θ−n by this factor gives the conditional survivor probability density function
m−(n−1)∏i=j​1{0<xi​<m}​.
(12)
This factorization proves the claimed conditional independence; scaling removes m. Keep the surviving labels in a fixed order, or apply an independent random permutation. The sorted survivors instead have the joint law of uniform order statistics and exhibit statistical dependence; sorting does not affect their empirical distribution function. Delete the maximum itself, which would otherwise become a forced value 1, and compute the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic using sample size n−1 and jump heights i/(n−1). This gives an exact conditional Kolmogorov-Smirnov test under the uniform-endpoint statistical model. It does not justify fitting an arbitrary endpoint or other statistical parameters and using the ordinary n-sample calibration.

Statistical inference OurBigBook.com
All evidence in observed data about a parameter is contained in its likelihood function; proportional likelihoods carry the same evidence. If a stopping rule contributes only a positive factor independent of the parameter to the complete observed-sample likelihood, that factor does not change likelihood-based inference. Recording only a coarsened part of the sample produces a different likelihood and is not covered by the same invariance claim.

Its minimal sufficient statistic is (N,S) by the parameter-free likelihood-ratio criterion. If only the last value Y is recorded, its density instead is α(y)e−θy/∫0∞​α(x)e−θxdx. The stopping rule therefore changes the coarsened-data inference even though it adds no complete-data likelihood factor involving θ.

An efficient estimator attains a relevant information lower bound. A baseline-adjusted linear regression can improve precision in a randomized controlled trial by removing prognostic variation.

A statistical functional is pathwise differentiable relative to chosen statistical paths if its derivative along every path depends only on that path's score function and defines a bounded linear functional on their statistical tangent space. Scoring rule (S(P,x))

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Statistical inference OurBigBook.com
A scoring rule turns a probability distribution forecast and an observed outcome into a number. For example, a forecast of rain with probability 0.7 should express uncertainty more usefully than a bare prediction of rain. A scoring rule lets us compare such forecasts after observations arrive, and its choice determines whether exaggerating confidence pays. A proper scoring rule rewards an honest account of uncertainty in expected value.
There are two sign conventions. A reward S(P,x) is maximized; a loss function L(P,x) is minimized. The conversion L=−S reverses every comparison. Here the linear probability score is a reward, while the binary Brier score and the negative logarithmic scoring rule are losses. Calling all three a "score" without specifying the direction would hide the central difference.
Throughout the binary examples, the random variable Y has a Bernoulli distribution with actual success probability q=0.7, and the report p∈[0,1] assigns probability p to Y=1 and 1−p to Y=0. The value q=0.7 is stipulated by this statistical model; it is not inferred from data or a claim that a forecasting system is calibrated. In practice the true predictive distribution is unknown, and the relevant q is the conditional probability of success given the information available when the forecast is issued. Propriety evaluates incentives for reporting that predictive distribution; it does not supply the unknown probabilities.

Words: 140
Scoring rule OurBigBook.com
The linear probability score pays the reported probability of whichever binary outcome occurs. With report p and observed y∈{0,1}, its reward is
Slin​(p,y)=yp+(1−y)(1−p).
(14)
It looks sensible: assign more probability to what happens and receive more reward. But the expected value under a Bernoulli distribution with true success probability q is
Eq​[Slin​(p,Y)]=qp+(1−q)(1−p)=1−q+(2q−1)p.
(15)
This is an affine function of the report. When q>1/2, the maximum over [0,1] is at p=1; when q<1/2, it is at p=0. At q=1/2, every report ties. Thus the linear probability score encourages reporting certainty about the more likely outcome and is not a proper scoring rule.
For the stipulated q=0.7, the expected value of the reward is 0.3+0.4p. Honest reporting p=0.7 earns 0.58 in expectation, whereas p=1 earns 0.7. The forecaster improves expected reward by replacing a 70% forecast with a 100% forecast. The Brier score and logarithmic scoring rule avoid this incentive, as the expected-score diagram under proper scoring rule shows.

Words: 886 Articles: 4
Scoring rule OurBigBook.com
A proper scoring rule makes reporting the true probability distribution optimal in expected value, for every true probability distribution in the allowed class of forecasts. In the reward convention, the inequality in the title holds for every report P and true law Q. The expected value is always taken under Q, because the report does not change how the outcome is generated. In the loss convention the same definition reads
EQ​[L(Q,X)]≤EQ​[L(P,X)]for every admissible P,Q.
(16)
This requirement makes a proper scoring rule useful for eliciting probabilities and comparing predictive distributions: deliberately distorting a known forecast cannot improve its expected reward or expected loss. The reward convention and its strict version are set out in Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation by Tilmann Gneiting and others (Section 1).
For the Bernoulli distribution with q=0.7, the Brier score has expected loss (p−0.7)2+0.21, and the negative logarithmic scoring rule has expected loss −0.7lnp−0.3ln(1−p). Both are minimized at the honest report p=0.7. The linear probability score, by contrast, maximizes its expected reward at p=1. These are statements about averaging over both possible outcomes with their actual probabilities.
The left panel displays each excess expected loss divided by that rule's expected loss at p=q: 0.21 for the Brier score and approximately 0.610864 for the logarithmic scoring rule. This normalization permits comparison of curve shapes and preserves the minimizing report, since it subtracts a constant and divides by a positive constant independent of p. Zero means no excess expected loss. The right panel shows the unmodified linear probability score reward, with its maximizing direction labeled explicitly.

Strictly proper scoring rule

Words: 646 Articles: 3
Proper scoring rule OurBigBook.com
A strictly proper scoring rule is a proper scoring rule for which the true probability distribution is the unique optimizer of the expected value. Equivalently, any different admissible probability distribution gives strictly larger expected loss. For probability density functions, two densities that agree almost everywhere represent the same probability distribution. Ordinary propriety permits ties: the constant reward S(P,x)=0 is a proper scoring rule, because every report ties, but it is not a strictly proper scoring rule and elicits no information.
Strict propriety concerns expectation, not guaranteed success on each observation or each realized dataset. With the stipulated Bernoulli distribution q=0.7, suppose the outcome is Y=0. The honest report p=0.7 then has Brier score loss 0.49, while p=0.2 has loss 0.04. The logarithmic loss similarly gives losses −ln(0.3)≈1.203973 and −ln(0.8)≈0.223144. The honest forecast loses this comparison on that draw, which occurs with probability 0.3 in the stipulated statistical model.
The Y=0 loss curves favor p=0, and the Y=1 loss curves favor p=1. Their weighted average, with weights 0.3 and 0.7, favors p=0.7. Choosing a report after observing Y would use information unavailable at forecast time. Even an average loss on a finite dataset can rank an honest forecast below a competing forecast through outcome variation; strict propriety guarantees the ranking in expected value under the specified information and true predictive distribution.
Brier score (LB​(p,y)=(p−y)2)
Words: 203
Strictly proper scoring rule OurBigBook.com
The binary Brier score applies squared-error loss to a reported success probability p and the observed indicator y∈{0,1}. It is a loss, so smaller is better. Its values lie in [0,1]: predicting the outcome with certainty gives zero, while assigning it zero probability gives one. Unlike the logarithmic scoring rule loss, the binary Brier score remains bounded even for a confidently wrong forecast.
For a Bernoulli distribution with true success probability q, averaging the two squared losses gives
Eq​[(p−Y)2]=q(p−1)2+(1−q)p2=(p−q)2+q(1−q).
(17)
The report controls only (p−q)2; the remaining term is the variance of the Bernoulli random variable. Consequently the Brier score is a strictly proper scoring rule. At q=0.7, the expected loss is (p−0.7)2+0.21, with unique minimum 0.21 at p=0.7. Reporting p=0.2 instead gives expected loss 0.46, despite its better loss on the particular outcome Y=0 above.
For several possible categories, the Brier score sums the squared differences between reported probabilities and observed category indicators. With two categories that sum is 2(p−y)2, so its numerical values are twice the binary convention used here, with the same optimizing report. Brier's original [ref] averages these category-sum losses over forecasts. Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation by Tilmann Gneiting and others (Section 3.1, Example 1, and Table 1) gives the category-sum and binary forms as negative rewards; negating them gives the losses described here.
Logarithmic scoring rule (S(p,y)=logp(y))
Words: 236 Articles: 1
Strictly proper scoring rule OurBigBook.com
The logarithmic scoring rule rewards the natural logarithm of the reported probability mass or probability density at the observed outcome. The title uses the reward convention. For a binary report p, its negative is the logarithmic loss:
Llog​(p,y)=−ylnp−(1−y)ln(1−p),0<p<1.
(18)
For y=1 this is −lnp; for y=0 it is −ln(1−p). At an endpoint, use these outcome-specific forms: assigning zero probability to the outcome incurs infinite loss, while assigning it probability one gives zero. The natural logarithm therefore makes a confidently wrong binary forecast far more costly than the bounded Brier score does.
Under the stipulated Bernoulli distribution with q=0.7, the expected logarithmic loss is
E0.7​[Llog​(p,Y)]=−0.7lnp−0.3ln(1−p).
(19)
Its unique minimum is at p=0.7, where the expected loss is approximately 0.610864. At p=0.2 it is approximately 1.193550. More generally, the excess expected logarithmic loss over truthful reporting is the Kullback-Leibler divergence in the order true law first, reported law second:
Eq​[Llog​(p,Y)]−Eq​[Llog​(q,Y)]=qlnpq​+(1−q)ln1−p1−q​=DKL​(Bernoulli(q)∥Bernoulli(p)).
(20)
For 0<q<1, this Kullback-Leibler divergence is nonnegative and vanishes only at p=q, explaining why the logarithmic scoring rule is a strictly proper scoring rule. The same Kullback-Leibler divergence identity applies to probability density functions relative to a common measure when the truthful expected logarithmic loss is finite and the comparison expected value is well defined.[ref] For sequential forecasts, the existing prequential log score identity explains how logarithmic rewards add over observations.

A statistic is complete for a parameter family if the displayed implication holds for every measurable g integrable under all parameter values. This property does not itself assert sufficiency; a complete sufficient statistic has both properties. Bounded completeness requires the defining implication for a complete statistic only for bounded measurable functions. Completeness implies it, but the converse need not hold. Meta-analysis

Words: 1k Articles: 25
Statistical inference OurBigBook.com
A meta-analysis combines statistical evidence from several studies addressing a common estimand. It may assume a shared effect or use a random-effects meta-analysis to represent between-study variation. Inverse-variance weighted means combine independent effect estimates when their variances are known or estimated; differences in study validity and effect modifiers require substantive assessment, not just weighting.

Meta-analysis OurBigBook.com
Divide studies by a specified characteristic and estimate an effect in each subgroup, then test the difference using an independent subgroup contrast in meta-analysis or an appropriate interaction model. The test of a between-group difference is distinct from separate tests against no effect within each group. Exploratory splits can be affected by multiple testing and by confounding between study characteristics.

Meta-analysis OurBigBook.com
A forest plot shows each study's effect estimate and confidence interval, together with a pooled estimate when appropriate. A vertical null-effect line allows comparison on a common scale. For an odds ratio the null is one and a logarithmic axis treats reciprocal ratios symmetrically; marker areas commonly encode study weights.

Funnel plot

Words: 92 Articles: 1
Meta-analysis OurBigBook.com
A funnel plot displays study effect estimates against a measure of their precision, often standard error increasing down the vertical axis. Under a common-effect model, imprecise estimates spread more widely around the effect. Asymmetry is evidence of a small-study effect and can be consistent with publication bias, but it has other possible explanations.

Small-study effect

Words: 46
Funnel plot OurBigBook.com
A small-study effect is a systematic relationship between study precision or size and estimated effect. It may result from selective publication, design differences, effect modification or other heterogeneity. A regression of effect on its standard error tests one such relationship; it does not by itself determine which mechanism generated it.

Publication bias

Meta-analysis OurBigBook.com
Publication bias arises when the availability of studies depends on the results, such as their significance, magnitude or direction. A meta-analysis of the available studies can then differ systematically from one including all eligible evidence. Funnel plot asymmetry can motivate investigation but does not establish this mechanism; heterogeneity and other small-study effects can also cause asymmetry.

Publication bias OurBigBook.com
A selection model combines a distribution for all study results with a probability π(y) that a result becomes available. The observed distribution is reweighted by this probability and renormalized. Assumed or estimated selection mechanisms permit sensitivity analysis of a meta-analysis, but unavailable results generally prevent a fully assumption-free correction.
Odds under at-least-one-positive selection (Rn​=R[1−βn]/[1−(1−α)n])

Selection model for publication bias OurBigBook.com
For n studies conditionally independent given the truth of one relationship, the event that at least one is positive has probability 1−βn under the alternative and 1−(1−α)n under the null. Its Bayes factor therefore gives the displayed posterior odds. For interior error probabilities these tend back to the prior odds R. If power exceeds size, the Bayes factor decreases to one: the quotient of geometric sums is a weighted average of decreasing powers [β/(1−α)]k.
This result concerns the coarsened selection event. Full observed results instead multiply their individual Bayes factors, and concordant evidence can accumulate without this bound. It is a useful example of information discarded by publication bias.

Trim and fill estimates missing studies from funnel plot asymmetry by trimming extreme studies to locate a centre and filling in counterparts on the less represented side. Its interpretation depends on a symmetry model for missing evidence; it is not a guarantee that genuine publication bias has been removed.

Statistical consistency is an implication of suitable transitivity and modeling assumptions, not a substitute for assessing them.

For median regression, a(θ)=θ2/(1+θ4) has unique zero at zero, but a small positive fitted sample median c has a second solution θ2=(1+1−4c2​)/(2c). This solution diverges as c↓0, although uniform convergence on any fixed compact interval holds. Constraining the estimator, or proving suitable global separation and localization, repairs the argument.

Influence function (IF(x;T,F))

Words: 2k Articles: 14
Robust statistics OurBigBook.com
An influence function asks how much a population answer moves when an infinitesimal fraction of its probability distribution is relocated to a specified point. It distinguishes the unbounded response of the mean from the bounded response of the median and the Huber location estimator. The normal-location influence curves and finite contamination bias of normal location below make that difference quantitative.
Let T be a real-valued statistical functional, F a reference probability measure, and δx​ the Dirac measure concentrated at x. Along the epsilon-contamination neighborhood path Fε,x​=(1−ε)F+εδx​, define the right derivative
IF(x;T,F)=limε↓0​εT(Fε,x​)−T(F)​,T(Fε,x​)=T(F)+εIF(x;T,F)+o(ε).
(26)
The name influence curve refers to the same object. The derivative is in the signed direction δx​−F, so the calculation removes baseline mass as well as adding a Dirac measure. The definition is a limit for each fixed x; it does not automatically give a remainder uniform over arbitrarily distant x.[ref]
The statistical functional must be defined on these contaminated probability measures, and the right derivative must exist and be finite. For a mean, a finite first absolute moment suffices. For a median, require a unique baseline median and a probability density function continuous and strictly positive there. For a smooth M-estimator, require an isolated population root, justified differentiation of its expected value, and a nonzero derivative with respect to the fitted parameter. These are specific conditions for the formulas below. Existence of the pointwise influence function alone proves neither an asymptotic linear representation nor pathwise differentiability of a statistical functional; each needs control of its own remainder and admissible statistical paths.

Influence function of the mean (IF(x;μ,F)=x−μ)

Words: 141
Influence function OurBigBook.com
For the statistical functional T(F)=μ=EF​X, assuming EF​∣X∣<∞, the contaminated mean is exactly
T(Fε,x​)=(1−ε)μ+εx.
(27)
Thus the influence function of the mean is x−μ, and its gross-error sensitivity is infinite on an unbounded sample space. The linear approximation is exact here: any fixed positive contamination fraction allows an arbitrarily large change by moving x far enough. No finite second moment is needed for this derivative, although a finite variance is needed for the usual central limit theorem for the sample mean.
For comparison, the influence function of the sample median is
IF(x;Med,F)=2f(m)sgn(x−m)​,x=m,
(28)
when the median m is unique and the probability density function f is positive and continuous at m. The sign function records which side of m receives the contaminating mass. The influence function of a quantile supplies the short derivation. With the generalized-inverse quantile convention, contamination exactly at x=m leaves the median at m, giving derivative zero there. If f(m) is very small, this bounded influence function can still be large; if f(m)=0, the displayed formula is unavailable.

Influence function of a Huber location estimator (IF(x;T,F)=sψk​((x−θ)/s)/A)

Words: 273
Influence function OurBigBook.com
Fix a scale s>0 and cutoff k>0. Define the population Huber location estimator by the root
EF​ψk​(sX−θ​)=0,θ=T(F),A=EF​ψk′​(sX−θ​)>0.
(29)
Here ψk​ is the Huber score. It has Lipschitz continuity, so dominated convergence justifies differentiation when F puts no mass at θ±ks. Then A=PF​(∣X−θ∣<ks), and the nonzero derivative identifies the local population root. The implicit function theorem applies away from the contaminating score's kinks; its Lipschitz continuity also gives the first-order expansion at those kinks. Differentiating its contaminated equation yields
0=−sA​IF(x;T,F)+ψk​(sx−θ​),IF(x;T,F)=Asψk​((x−θ)/s)​.
(30)
The normalization matters: the Huber score alone is not the influence function. The gross-error sensitivity is sk/A, while the rejection point of an influence function is infinite because the clipped tails stay nonzero. The original clipped estimating criterion and its derivative normalization also appear in the population analysis of M-estimators.[ref]
Scale sets what counts as a large residual. For a normal distribution N(μ,σ2) with fixed s=σ, symmetry gives θ=μ and A=2Φ(k)−1, where Φ is the standard normal distribution function. If the scale is instead a statistical functional S(F), differentiation of the joint equation adds the scale contribution:
IF(x;T,F)=Asψk​(rx​)−BIF(x;S,F)​,rx​=sx−θ​,B=EF​[rX​ψk′​(rX​)].
(31)
Under a symmetric baseline and an odd Huber score, B=0, so scale estimation drops out at first order. This cancellation needs regularity of S and does not protect finite contamination changes: an inflated standard deviation enlarges the physical cutoff ks. A robust choice, such as a suitable Scale M-estimator, needs its own influence function and breakdown point checked. Fixing a numeric cutoff in raw units also sacrifices scale equivariance when units change.[ref]

Local influence versus replacement breakdown

Words: 244
Influence function OurBigBook.com
The influence function describes an infinitesimal change at a specified reference probability distribution. The replacement breakdown point asks how many observations in a particular finite sample can be replaced before an estimator becomes unbounded. The finite-sample maximum bias records the intervening changes. These are different questions: a bounded influence function at one baseline is not a general bound over all epsilon-contamination neighborhoods, nor a proof of a positive replacement breakdown point.[ref]
The mean illustrates agreement between local and global fragility: its gross-error sensitivity is infinite and one replacement can send the sample mean arbitrarily far. The median has finite gross-error sensitivity under the stated positive-density assumptions, while its sample median withstands fewer than about half the observations being replaced under ordinary tie conventions. Its population contamination bias above still diverges as ε↑1/2 when the atom remains beyond the shifted median. Here x must also move outward; taking that limit with a fixed finite atom would invalidate the displayed quantile formula.
For scalar location with a fixed positive scale, the Huber score has a direct global argument: if strictly more than half of the sample stays fixed, then beyond every retained observation by more than ks, their saturated scores outweigh all possible replaced scores. Every root therefore stays in a bounded interval. This is a separate finite-replacement argument; estimating scale changes its premises. A smooth bounded influence function is valuable local protection, but global robustness also depends on the full estimating rule, scale choice, and root selection.

Boundedness of the influence function does not imply a finite rejection point: the influence function of a quantile has nonzero constant tails. Nor does tending to zero at infinity guarantee a finite rejection point unless those tails become identically zero.

Words: 366 Articles: 4
Statistical decision theory OurBigBook.com
Cost-effectiveness analysis compares interventions through their costs and effects measured in a common outcome unit. Let ΔC and ΔE denote mean differences relative to a specified comparator. A positive effect increment with nonpositive cost increment gives dominance; the reverse signs give a dominated intervention. A tradeoff in the positive-positive quadrant requires a willingness-to-pay threshold per outcome unit. Randomized controlled trials can estimate these differences, but their joint sampling distribution is needed to express uncertainty. Outcome units, time horizon and costing perspective must be specified; a survival-day increment is not automatically a quality-adjusted outcome.

It avoids dividing by a potentially near-zero or negative effect estimate. For estimates with variances vE​,vC​ and covariance vCE​, its estimated variance is λ2vE​+vC​−2λvCE​. A normal approximation therefore gives a confidence interval directly on the net-benefit scale. The economic sign criterion does not require a positive effect increment.

Under a posterior distribution this is a posterior probability. A frequentist paired bootstrap version displays the fraction of replicates for which the net benefit is positive, a resampling measure of uncertainty rather than literally a probability that a fixed true parameter is positive. Using the sign of net benefit handles all quadrants of the cost-effectiveness plane; counting only replicates whose ratio is below the threshold does not.

A threshold λ corresponds to the line ΔC=λΔE; points below the line have positive incremental net monetary benefit, in every quadrant. A joint confidence region or paired bootstrap cloud reveals uncertainty and preserves the dependence between cost and effect estimates.

When ΔE<0 the inequality reverses on division, and when ΔE=0 the ratio is undefined. A ratio alone cannot identify the quadrant of the cost-effectiveness plane.

Confidence interval (C(X)=[L(X),U(X)])

Words: 2k Articles: 11
Statistical inference OurBigBook.com
A confidence interval is a random interval constructed from a statistical sample to cover a fixed unknown statistical parameter with a prescribed coverage probability. For a scalar target θ, a procedure with nominal confidence 1−α satisfies
Pθ​{L(X)≤θ≤U(X)}≥1−αfor every admissible θ.
(45)
The subscript records which probability distribution generates the repeated samples. The endpoints are statistics, so they vary from sample to sample; the target is fixed. Equality gives exact nominal coverage probability, while the inequality also permits conservative procedures. For a general estimand ψ(θ), replace the target inside the interval by ψ(θ).
A realized confidence interval communicates the precision of an estimate in the target's own units. Reporting 1.2 alone conceals the difference between an estimate with standard error 0.5 and one with standard error 0.05. A narrow confidence interval indicates greater precision for the stated statistical model, rather than a guarantee that its assumptions describe the experiment correctly.
Once x is observed, C(x) either contains the fixed target or does not. The 95% statement concerns the random procedure C(X), not a posterior probability of 0.95 that this particular interval contains θ. A credible interval instead assigns specified posterior probability to a region under Bayesian inference. These interpretations can differ even when the numerical endpoints agree. The repeated-sampling interpretation is explained in NIST's confidence-limits teaching reference.
Jerzy Neyman's 1937 paper formulates the fixed-target, random-endpoint construction in Section II, especially equation (20) on page 348. Its confidence coefficient must hold across the allowed statistical parameters, rather than only at the value suggested by one sample. See Neyman, Outline of a Theory of Statistical Estimation Based on the Classical Theory of Probability and the original paper scan.

Confidence interval OurBigBook.com
Suppose X1​,…,Xn​ are independent and identically distributed with normal distribution N(μ,σ2), where the mean μ is unknown and the standard deviation σ>0 is known. The sample mean Xˉ=n−1∑i​Xi​ has normal distribution N(μ,σ2/n) and standard error σ/n​. With zq​ the standard normal quantile at q, the displayed confidence interval has exact coverage probability 1−α for every μ and every positive integer n. No central limit theorem approximation is needed.
Take σ=2, n=16 and nominal confidence 95%. The standard error is 2/16​=0.5, and z0.975​=1.9599639845…. Therefore
C(X)=[Xˉ−0.9799819923…, Xˉ+0.9799819923…].
(46)
Rounded for reporting, this is xˉ±0.98. If xˉ=1.2, the realized confidence interval is approximately [0.22,2.18]. Exact 95% calibration refers to the unrounded standard normal quantile; using 1.96 literally gives coverage probability 0.9500042097…, almost but not exactly 0.95.
The confidence interval's width scales as n−1/2: increasing sample size from 16 to 64 halves its half-width to 0.4899909961…. If σ is unknown, merely substituting the square root of a sample variance loses the displayed exact calibration; for the same normal distribution model, use a Student t confidence interval.
The figure holds the true mean at μ=0 and independently generates 40 samples of 16 observations from the same normal distribution. NumPy's PCG64 generator with seed 42 gives 39 covering confidence intervals and one miss, at sample 32: observed coverage is 39/40=97.5%. Every bar uses the unrounded standard normal quantile. This finite collection illustrates the moving endpoints; it does not establish the analytic coverage probability or require exactly two misses.
The beauty of the construction is that a familiar standard normal distribution calibrates every possible unknown mean at once. For a short proof, the pivotal quantity
Z=σ/n​Xˉ−μ​∼N(0,1)
(47)
has a probability distribution independent of μ. The event ∣Z∣≤z1−α/2​ has probability 1−α; rearranging it gives μ∈C(X). The right panel shows the equivalent event ∣Xˉ∣≤0.9799819923… when μ=0.

Under the null hypothesis, the standardized test statistic has standard normal distribution. Write Φ for the standard normal distribution function. With xˉ=1.2, σ=2, n=16 and μ0​=0, the observed test statistic is z=1.2/0.5=2.4. Its p-value is
p=Pμ0​​(∣Z∣≥2.4)=2[1−Φ(2.4)]=0.01639507185….
(48)
Thus the p-value is a tail probability computed under the null hypothesis, including departures in both directions. It is not P(H0​∣x), the posterior probability of the null hypothesis, nor the probability that the observations arose "by chance". The normal distribution test statistic and its calibration appear in NIST's teaching reference for testing a process mean; the tail interpretation is stated in Penn State's hypothesis-testing notes.
Choose the significance level α=0.05 before observing the sample. The rejection region is ∣Z∣>z0.975​, whose probability under H0​ is exactly 0.05. Here 2.4>1.9599639845…, so reject H0​. This agrees with zero lying outside [0.22,2.18]. More generally, a proposed μ0​ belongs to the unrounded 95% confidence interval precisely when its two-sided test does not reject under this strict cutoff. The equality boundary has probability zero in this continuous statistical model.
The significance level and statistical power describe different repeated-experiment probabilities. At a specified alternative μ, put δ=(μ−μ0​)/(σ/n​) and q=z1−α/2​. Then
Pμ0​​(reject H0​)β(μ)=Pμ​(do not reject H0​)Pμ​(reject H0​)​=α,=Φ(q−δ)−Φ(−q−δ),=1−β(μ).​
(49)
The first is the Type I error probability; the second is the Type II error probability at that alternative. For a planning alternative μ=1, keeping μ0​=0, σ=2 and n=16 gives δ=2, β(1)≈0.483995 and statistical power 0.516005. At n=64, δ=4 and statistical power rises to 0.979327. These are model calculations for specified alternatives, not posterior probabilities inferred from a nonsignificant result. They explain why failure to reject cannot establish equality and why choosing sample size before an experiment is useful.
Historically, Ronald Fisher's 1925 book discusses the normal cutoff 1.96 and tail probability 0.05 as a convenient convention on page 47, rather than a mathematically compulsory threshold: [ref].

Coverage probability (Pθ​(θ∈C(Y)))

Confidence interval OurBigBook.com
The coverage probability is the repeated-sampling probability that a random confidence interval contains the fixed true statistical parameter. A finite-sample level-1−α procedure has coverage probability at least 1−α at every admissible statistical parameter; exact nominal coverage means equality. An asymptotically calibrated procedure approaches the nominal value as sample size grows, under its stated assumptions. Higher-order Edgeworth expansions can quantify the discrepancy from nominal coverage probability when their regularity conditions hold.
Observed coverage in finitely many repetitions is itself random. For m independent repetitions of the exact normal mean confidence interval with known variance, the count K of covering confidence intervals has binomial distribution Binomial(m,0.95). At m=40, its expectation is 38, but
P(K=39)=(3940​)0.95390.05≈0.270552.
(50)
Consequently, the 39 successes in the figure are compatible with exact 95% coverage probability. The guarantee follows from the pivotal quantity's probability distribution; the finite observed fraction is an illustration. Also distinguish a confidence interval for a fixed mean from a prediction interval for a future observation: the latter must accommodate the new observation's variation as well as estimation uncertainty.

Bayesian statistics

Words: 8k Articles: 156
Statistical inference OurBigBook.com
Bayesian statistics expresses uncertainty about an unknown statistical parameter through a probability distribution, then uses Bayes' theorem to update it after observing data. The prior distribution describes uncertainty before the current observations; the likelihood function describes how the statistical model generates those observations at each parameter value; the posterior distribution describes uncertainty conditional on the observations and that model. A physical parameter can have one fixed value while its value remains uncertain to us. Assigning it a probability distribution represents that uncertainty under the chosen model, rather than requiring the physical parameter to change randomly between measurements.
For example, suppose ten Bernoulli trials are independent conditional on an unknown heads probability θ, with a beta distribution prior Beta(2,2). Eight heads and two tails give the posterior distribution Beta(10,4) by Beta-binomial conjugacy. Its posterior mean is 10/14=5/7≈0.714286, between the prior mean 1/2 and observed binomial proportion 8/10. The Bayesian posterior below computes the whole update, and the credible interval below summarizes its remaining uncertainty. The conjugate update is explained in MIT 18.05, Reading 15: beta and normal conjugate priors.
The useful feature is that one posterior distribution supports several questions: a posterior mean estimates a value, a credible interval reports a range, and a posterior predictive distribution predicts a future observation while averaging over parameter uncertainty. With conditionally independent new data, today's posterior distribution can become tomorrow's prior distribution. These conclusions remain conditional on the statistical model and prior distribution; a precise update does not establish that either assumption fits the experiment.
A historical starting point is Thomas Bayes's essay in the 1763 volume of the Royal Society's Philosophical Transactions, communicated after his death by Richard Price. Its opening problem asks for uncertainty about an unknown event probability given observed successes and failures: the same direction of reasoning illustrated by the coin example. See Bayes and Price, An Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances, opening letter and problem.

Likelihood reconstruction from posterior simulation

Words: 74
Bayesian statistics OurBigBook.com
For data x, a positive prior distribution density π and likelihood function ℓ, Bayes' theorem gives posterior density h(θ∣x)=π(θ)ℓ(θ)/m(x). Thus h/π reconstructs the likelihood up to a constant. Estimate the posterior density from simulation, divide by the known prior density and maximize over the search region. A posterior mode alone instead estimates a maximum a posteriori estimate; it estimates a likelihood maximizer only when the prior is constant there. Prior support must include the likelihood maximizer of interest.

A credible interval is an interval C(d) containing a prescribed amount 1−α of posterior probability for an unknown scalar statistical parameter Θ. For a continuous posterior distribution with posterior density p(θ∣d), its endpoints satisfy
P(a≤Θ≤b∣D=d)=∫ab​p(θ∣d)dθ=1−α.
(55)
The conditioning includes the chosen statistical model and prior distribution. For a discrete posterior distribution, exact equality may be impossible because of its probability masses; an interval can instead be required to contain at least the requested posterior probability. An interval compresses the full posterior distribution into a range whose uncertainty can be communicated in the parameter's own units. See MIT 18.05, Class 16: probability intervals.
For the eight-head, two-tail example in Bayesian statistics, the posterior density is 2860θ9(1−θ)3 on [0,1]. Its cumulative distribution function, obtained by integration of this polynomial, is
F(t)=286t10−780t11+715t12−220t13,0≤t≤1.
(56)
Solving F(a)=0.025 and F(b)=0.975 by the bisection method gives
a≈0.461868461,b≈0.909079605,F(b)−F(a)=0.95.
(57)
These are numerical approximations to the exact quantiles defined by those equations; the endpoints were computed from the cumulative distribution function, rather than read off a plot. The resulting equal-tailed credible interval leaves 2.5% posterior probability on each side. Its shaded area is 95% of the total area under the posterior density.
Credible intervals are not unique. The one-sided credible interval [0,F−1(0.95)]≈[0,0.887334219] also has 95% posterior probability, but leaves all 5% outside it on the right. A highest density region instead selects points above a density threshold; it need not be an equal-tailed credible interval, and when the posterior density has separated peaks it need not be one interval at all. Thus a reported credible interval should specify its construction.
A 95% credible interval makes a statement about the statistical parameter conditional on these observed data and the Bayesian model. A 95% confidence interval instead refers to the coverage probability of a procedure under repeated sampling at a fixed parameter value. These are different conditioning statements: 95% posterior probability does not by itself imply 95% coverage probability for every fixed parameter. The confidence interval article develops that sampling interpretation.

Before the same eight heads and two tails, a uniform prior Beta(1,1) would give posterior mean 9/12=3/4, compared with 5/7 under Beta(2,2): the observations do not uniquely determine a Bayesian posterior. Even a uniform prior makes a choice of parameter coordinates; its child article explains why changing coordinates can destroy uniformity.

Bayes' theorem gives

The Bayesian model evidence m(d) is the normalization constant making the posterior density integrate to one. The strict positive, finite condition is essential: a zero or infinite normalizer does not define this posterior distribution, even if the unnormalized expression can be written down. Other reference measures give the corresponding density formula; discrete parameter values replace the integral by a sum. The posterior propriety article gives examples where normalization fails.
With d fixed, L(θ;d)=p(d∣θ) is a likelihood function of θ. Its normalization as a sampling distribution is over possible data, not over parameter values. In particular, a likelihood function is not a probability density function for Θ and need not integrate to one over θ. The prior density supplies the probability weighting, and the Bayesian model evidence normalizes their product. This distinction prevents a tempting mistake: reversing the conditioning merely by exchanging the words “data” and “parameter”.
For eight heads among ten conditionally independent Bernoulli trials, take the observed data to be the heads count D=8. Its binomial distribution likelihood function and the Beta(2,2) prior density give

Thus the posterior distribution is Beta(10,4). If the data are instead one particular ordered sequence with eight heads and two tails, its likelihood function omits the factor 45 and its Bayesian model evidence becomes 3/1430. The factor cancels in Bayes' theorem, leaving the same posterior distribution; these two data descriptions have different sampling probabilities but identical information about θ here.
The prior density and posterior density use the left axis and each integrate to one. The dashed likelihood function uses the right axis and is divided by its maximum solely to compare its shape; it is not a parameter probability density function. The likelihood function peaks at 8/10, while the posterior mode is 9/12=3/4 and the posterior mean is 5/7. Multiplying by the prior density shifts the preferred values toward one half while preserving a range of possibilities.
The resulting posterior variance is 10⋅4/(142⋅15)=2/147≈0.0136054, compared with prior variance 1/20. In this example the update reduces uncertainty. The posterior predictive probability of heads on the next conditionally independent toss is E[Θ∣D=8]=5/7, and the credible interval above reports a 95% range. These are summaries of the same posterior distribution, rather than competing estimates of one density peak.

Very small random-walk proposals give high acceptance but slow diffusion; very large proposals produce low acceptance and repeated states. Markov chain Monte Carlo OurBigBook.com
Coupling from the past uses a fixed two-sided sequence of random update maps for a finite Markov chain. Increase a backward horizon until the composition from that horizon to time zero sends every starting state to the same state. Retain the maps at previously exposed times. The resulting common image is an exact stationary sample. If a length-m block has positive probability ε of mapping every state to one state, independent disjoint blocks imply failure to coalesce by horizon T has probability at most (1−ε)⌊T/m⌋. For a deterministic horizon, a stationary initial state yields a stationary final state, and agrees with the algorithm's output on coalescence. Letting the deterministic horizon tend to infinity proves the output has the stationary law without conditioning on a random stopping horizon.

For ferromagnetic Ising heat-bath updates, use the same updated vertex and uniform variable in every chain; the conditional probability of +1 increases with every neighbour's spin. A block visiting all vertices once with all uniforms below the least conditional probability of +1 maps every state to all plus, proving almost-sure termination.

Trends suggest an initial transient or slow exploration, separated regimes suggest transitions between posterior regions, and exact plateaus show repeated states. To update a positive parameter, a symmetric additive proposal distribution can be generated on the whole real line. Reject nonpositive proposals; accept positive ones using the target density ratio. The off-diagonal proposal remains symmetric. Repeatedly redrawing until the proposal is positive instead truncates and renormalizes the proposal differently at different current states, so a Hastings correction is then required. A symmetric walk in logv is another valid method, but its transformed target includes the Jacobian determinant factor v.
Proposal scale and random-walk Metropolis efficiency
Words: 67
Random-walk Metropolis algorithm OurBigBook.com
A small proposal scale increases acceptance while making successive states almost equal. A large scale often proposes low-density states and creates long rejection runs. A pilot comparison can optimize effective sample size of a Markov chain per unit computing time, or expected accepted squared displacement, rather than acceptance alone. Tune on representative functions and then fix the scale for production; an arbitrarily history-dependent adaptation is not automatically a chain with the desired invariant distribution.

Metropolis–Hastings algorithm OurBigBook.com
An independence Metropolis–Hastings algorithm proposes from a fixed density q independent of the current state. If supx​π(x)/q(x)<∞, it is uniformly and hence geometrically ergodic.

For a stationary Markov chain and a scalar observable with summable autocorrelation function ρ(k), the asymptotic variance of its sample mean is Var(h)τint​/n. Thus the effective sample size of a Markov chain is approximately n/τint​. Different observables can have very different autocorrelation times.

In a systematic Gibbs sampler for a standardized bivariate normal distribution with correlation ρ, update Z1​ conditionally on the old Z2​, then update Z2​ using the new Z1​. Substitution gives the displayed autoregressive process of order one, with independent noises with the standard normal distribution η1,r​,η2,r​. The sweep-to-sweep autocorrelation of Z2​ at lag h is ρ2h, so the chain mixes slowly as ∣ρ∣ approaches one.

Gibbs sampler OurBigBook.com
For a standard bivariate normal distribution with correlation ρ, each conditional has variance 1−ρ2 and mean ρ times the other coordinate. A sweep draws Xn+1​=ρYn​+1−ρ2​Z1​, then Yn+1​=ρXn+1​+1−ρ2​Z2​. The resulting coordinate chain is an AR(1) process with coefficient ρ2 and innovation variance 1−ρ4. It shows explicitly why near-unit correlation slows successive Gibbs sweeps.

Software for Bayesian inference through Markov chain Monte Carlo in directed statistical models. Its model language uses dnorm(mean, precision), so the second argument is inverse variance; dcat indexes a supplied probability vector, and dbern introduces a binary latent variable. The model is declarative, so the order of deterministic node definitions does not impose procedural evaluation order.

Gibbs sampler OurBigBook.com
For Gaussian precision (AC​CD​), a systematic update of the first coordinate followed by the second makes the centered second coordinate an AR(1) chain with coefficient C2/(AD)<1. Independent conditional Gaussian noise supplies its stable innovation. This proves convergence of the Gaussian Gibbs sampler and explains slower mixing when posterior correlation has magnitude near one.
Gibbs sampling for a finite hidden spin field
Words: 76 Articles: 1
Gibbs sampler OurBigBook.com
For a strictly positive posterior on finitely many binary spins, a Random-scan Gibbs sampler uses the two local posterior weights to redraw one spin. Positive full conditional distribution probabilities allow every finite sequence of spin changes, giving an irreducible Markov chain with positive self-transition probabilities.
Local likelihood factors in a hidden spin field
Words: 40
Gibbs sampling for a finite hidden spin field OurBigBook.com
When an observation mean depends on the neighboring spins, changing a spin affects observations centered at its neighbors. Its own observation need not involve that spin. Selecting precisely the affected factors gives a correct local full conditional distribution without recomputing the entire posterior.
Systematic Gibbs sampling need not be reversible
Words: 36
Gibbs sampler OurBigBook.com
Every full-conditional coordinate update satisfies detailed balance with the target distribution. Their systematic ordered composition preserves the target but need not satisfy detailed balance, since compositions of reversible kernels need not be reversible. A fixed-probability random-scan mixture remains reversible.
Blocked Gibbs sampler
Words: 70 Articles: 1
Gibbs sampler OurBigBook.com
A blocked Gibbs sampler draws groups of coordinates jointly from their full conditional distributions. Each update preserves the joint probability distribution; dependence between blocks can still cause a long mixing time.
Checkerboard Gibbs sampling
Words: 47
Blocked Gibbs sampler OurBigBook.com
On a bipartite image graph, the pixels of one color are conditionally independent given the other color. Draw all black pixels from their independent full conditionals, then draw all whites conditional on the new blacks. Each color update preserves the target law, so their composition does too.
Random-scan Gibbs sampler
Words: 77 Articles: 1
Gibbs sampler OurBigBook.com
A random-scan Gibbs sampler chooses one coordinate, commonly uniformly at random, and redraws it from its complete conditional distribution while leaving all other coordinates fixed. Each coordinate update preserves the target distribution.
Detailed balance of a random-scan Gibbs sampler
Words: 45
Random-scan Gibbs sampler OurBigBook.com
A single-coordinate Gibbs sampler update preserves the remaining coordinates and independently redraws the selected coordinate from its full conditional distribution. The joint measure of old and new states factors into a marginal and two identical conditional factors, making it symmetric. A fixed-probability mixture of such kernels therefore satisfies detailed balance.
Tempered Gibbs sampler
Words: 36
Gibbs sampler OurBigBook.com
A tempered Gibbs sampler changes the coordinate-selection probabilities and compensates by drawing from modified complete conditionals. Its invariant law can differ from the desired target, so expectations under the target are recovered with explicit importance weights.

Prior predictive check

Words: 53
Bayesian model evidence OurBigBook.com
A prior predictive check simulates parameters from the prior distribution and observations from their sampling model, then examines whether those observations are plausible before conditioning on data. This reveals unintended information from apparently broad priors, especially after nonlinear transformations or when scales and correlations are coupled. It differs from a posterior predictive check, which uses the posterior distribution.

Uniform-alternative binomial Bayes factor (B01​(y)=(n+1)(yn​)2−n)
Words: 71
Bayes factor OurBigBook.com
For a binomial distribution count, compare a point null θ=1/2 with the uniform alternative prior distribution on (0,1). The alternative Bayesian model evidence is
(yn​)∫01​θy(1−θ)n−ydθ=n+11​,
(87)
so the exact Bayes factor favouring the point null is (n+1)(yn​)2−n. With standardized deviation z=2(y−n/2)/n​, the local normal distribution approximation is B01​≈2n/π​e−z2/2. At fixed z the frequentist p-value remains approximately constant, while the factor grows like n​. This demonstrates the prior-width mechanism behind the Jeffreys-Lindley paradox for a Gaussian point null in a discrete sampling model.
Gaussian practical-null mixture
Words: 79
Bayes factor OurBigBook.com
A Gaussian practical-null mixture compares a narrow centered normal distribution prior with a wider centered normal distribution prior. Neither component is a point mass. With observed mean y∣β∼N(β,1/n) and prior precisions q0​>q1​>0, its model predictive variances are Vi​=1/n+1/qi​, and the Bayes factor is
B01​(y)=V1​/V0​​exp[−y2(V0−1​−V1−1​)/2].
(88)
The overall posterior density is a Bayesian model averaging mixture with component means ny/(n+qi​). A wide-prior penalty can favor the practical null near zero; its dominance depends quantitatively on both prior scales and the observation, not merely on the observation being of order n−1/2.

Jackknife bias correction (TJ​=nTn​−(n−1)TJ​)

Words: 521 Articles: 3
Statistical inference OurBigBook.com
The jackknife bias correction uses jackknife resampling to estimate and subtract the bias of an estimator. Here Tn​ denotes the original estimator, T(−i)​ its version after deleting observation i, and TJ​=n−1∑i=1n​T(−i)​ the mean of those versions. For sample size n>1, define
Bn​=(n−1)(TJ​−Tn​),TJ​=Tn​−Bn​=nTn​−(n−1)TJ​.
(90)
The sign matters: a negative estimated bias increases the corrected value. The original estimator and all deletion versions must target the same estimand and use the same estimation rule at their respective sample sizes. The definition alone does not make TJ​ an unbiased estimator.
For an exact worked example, take the empirical variance
Tn​=n1​∑i=1n​(Xi​−Xn​)2.
(91)
On (1,2,3,4,10), the sample mean is 4 and T5​=50/5=10. Each deletion empirical variance is recomputed around its own deletion sample mean, with divisor 4, giving
(T(−1)​,…,T(−5)​)=(9.6875,11.25,12.1875,12.5,1.25),TJ​=9.375.
(92)
For instance, deleting 10 leaves (1,2,3,4), whose sample mean is 2.5 and whose empirical variance is 1.25. The correction on the full statistical sample is
B5​=4(9.375−10)=−2.5,TJ​=10−(−2.5)=12.5.
(93)
The same data thus give a jackknife variance estimator of 2.5 for the sample mean, and a corrected empirical variance of 12.5; these are different estimands.
The exact equality with the usual sample variance is not an accident of these numbers. For any data with n>1, write Q=∑i​(xi​−x)2=nTn​. Removing xi​ changes this sum to Q−n(xi​−x)2/(n−1), so
T(−i)​=n−1Q​−(n−1)2n(xi​−x)2​,TJ​=(n−1)2n(n−2)​Tn​,TJ​=n−1n​Tn​=sn2​.
(94)
For independent and identically distributed random variables with finite second moment and population variance σ2, the expectation is ETn​=(1−1/n)σ2. Its bias is exactly −σ2/n; jackknife bias correction removes it exactly in this example. Thus sn2​ is an unbiased estimator of σ2 under these assumptions, including n=2 where each deletion empirical variance is zero.
More generally, suppose the bias has a regular expansion at both sample sizes n and n−1, with coefficients a,b independent of n:
Bn​=ETn​−θ=na​+n2b​+O(n−3).
(95)
Under independent and identically distributed sampling, each deletion estimator has the same expectation as Tn−1​. Hence the corrected bias is
ETJ​−θ=nBn​−(n−1)Bn−1​=O(n−2),nna​−(n−1)n−1a​=0.
(96)
The leading O(n−1) term cancels; the remaining bias need not vanish. The O notation is big O notation. This argument presumes the expansion, rather than proving it for every statistic; the regularity conditions discussed for the jackknife variance estimator and statistical dependence still require care. Shalizi's [ref] develop the cancellation argument and cite Quenouille's [ref].

Empirical variance (Tn​=n−1∑i=1n​(Xi​−Xn​)2)

Words: 35
Sample variance OurBigBook.com
The empirical variance is the variance of the empirical distribution, which puts probability 1/n on each observation. It uses divisor n, whereas the usual sample variance uses divisor n−1. For independent and identically distributed random variables with finite second moment, jackknife bias correction converts the empirical variance into the unbiased estimator sn2​ exactly.

Pooled sample variance (Sp2​=(SXX​+SYY​)/(m+n−2))

Words: 68
Sample variance OurBigBook.com
For two independent normal samples of sizes m,n with a common unknown variance, pooling their within-sample sums of squares gives the unbiased estimator Sp2​=(SXX​+SYY​)/(m+n−2). The numerator divided by the common population variance has a chi-squared distribution with m+n−2 degrees of freedom and is independent of both sample means. Therefore (Xˉ−Yˉ−(μX​−μY​))/(Sp​1/m+1/n​) has a Student t-distribution. This exact construction requires a positive residual number of degrees of freedom and the common-variance assumption.

Generalized estimating equation (∑i​DiT​Vi−1​(Yi​−mi​)=0)

Words: 293 Articles: 4
Estimating equation OurBigBook.com
For independent clusters with mean vector mi​(θ) and positive definite working covariance matrix Vi​, a generalized estimating equation solves
∑i​DiT​Vi−1​(Yi​−mi​)=0,Di​=∂mi​/∂θT.
(98)
Correct mean specification and regularity can give a consistent estimator of identifiable mean coefficients despite a misspecified working covariance. A sandwich covariance matrix accounts for actual cluster variation. Mean equations alone cannot identify two parameters that always enter through the same combination.

Working correlation matrix (Vi​=Ai1/2​Ri​(α)Ai1/2​)

Words: 56
Generalized estimating equation OurBigBook.com
A working correlation matrix Ri​(α) is a positive-definite proposed correlation structure used to weight a generalized estimating equation, with Ai​ the diagonal matrix of marginal variances. It need not equal the actual correlation matrix. Correct marginal means and independent sampling clusters keep the estimating equations unbiased; a cluster-level sandwich covariance matrix estimates their actual large-sample covariance. For three exchangeable observations, positive definiteness requires −1/2<ρ<1.

For independent subjects with repeated Bernoulli observations, specify marginal means mij​=logit−1(wijT​γ). A generalized estimating equation uses their derivative matrix Di​ and working covariance matrix Vi​ to solve ∑i​DiT​Vi−1​(Yi​−mi​)=0. Subject-level sandwich covariance matrices give robust uncertainty when the mean is correctly specified but the working correlation is not. The coefficients describe population odds ratios; this mean specification does not prescribe a complete joint distribution within a subject.

Words: 74
Population-averaged logistic model for repeated binary outcomes OurBigBook.com
For monotone missing data, let Rij​ indicate observation and let ρij​ be the product of the conditional retention probabilities through visit j. Under sequential missing at random, conditioning on the complete response history makes these retention probabilities depend only on the history already observed at each decision. Therefore E(Rij​/ρij​∣Yi​,Xi​)=1. Weighting a working-independence generalized estimating equation by Rij​/ρij​ restores its mean-zero property. This needs correct retention probabilities, positivity and regularity; uncertainty must account for estimating the weights.

A population-averaged log-rate model with exposure Pit​ gives an annual rate ratio eβ1​. Independent Poisson standard errors do not account for clustering. An exposure-weighted population rate and an equally weighted average of cluster rates are different estimands.

If a response has mean μ and variance V(μ), the delta method gives Var(g(Y))≈g′(μ)2V(μ). Choosing g′(μ) proportional to V(μ)−1/2 makes this first-order variance independent of μ. For Y∼N(μ,kμ2) with μ=0 and fixed k>0, represent Y=μ(1+k​Z) with Z having the standard normal distribution. Taking the natural logarithm of the absolute value gives the displayed identity. Its random second term has a common distribution, independent of μ, so this variance-stabilizing transformation gives an exactly constant variance. That variance is finite: the normal density is bounded near zero and ∫01​∣logt∣2dt<∞, while normal tails control logarithmic growth at infinity. The transformation is defined almost surely, loses the sign of the mean, and does not produce an exact normal distribution. A zero mean makes the original observation identically zero and is outside its domain.
